extracted.intended_audience: educated British public, statesmen, and policymakers (late 18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Political-essay guidance on forming and preserving a stable free government, addressing fiscal policy, the role of leaders, property, and constitutional prudence in the context of the French Revolution contrasted with the British Constitution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not trifle with the revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The revenue will not be trifled with. The prattling about the rights of men will not be accepted in payment of a biscuit or a pound of gunpowder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revenue and public finance are substantive necessities; rhetorical appeals or metaphysical speculation cannot substitute for real funds. Statesmen must treat public revenue as a serious obligation, not as a token or rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance acquisition and state demands
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep a balance between the power of acquisition on the part of the subject and the demands he is to answer on the part of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The means of acquisition are prior in time and arrangement; good order is the foundation of all good things. A true politician's skill is to maintain a proportion between private acquisition and public demands so that industry and conservation are preserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect property to preserve industry
rubrics_metrics.description: They must respect that property of which they cannot partake. Depriving people of their consolation in property deadens their industry and strikes at the root of all acquisition and conservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measures that undermine property rights reduce incentives to labor and accumulate fortune and thus harm the poor and the prosperous alike; protecting property is essential to economic health.

rubrics_metrics.name: Financial contrivances require a settled order
rubrics_metrics.description: Banks, circulations, annuities, tontines, perpetual rents, and like devices are good only when they assume the effects of that settled order and are built upon it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on mercantile or financial artifices as remedies for the breakdown of public order; such instruments function properly only within an established, lawful political and social framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid impractical fiscal schemes (e.g., coining church bells)
rubrics_metrics.description: Schemes like coining into money the bells of the suppressed churches are 'alchemy' and 'folly' that baffle argument and excite disgust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not adopt ostentatious or symbolic financial projects that have no sound basis in fiscal reality; such projects are deceptive and undermine confidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming a free government requires tempering liberty with restraint
rubrics_metrics.description: To form a free government — to temper together opposite elements of liberty and restraint in one consistent work — requires much thought, deep reflection, and a sagacious, powerful, and combining mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Giving freedom is easy; creating a stable free government is hard. It requires deliberate design to balance individual liberty and necessary restraints; neglecting this balance leads to either tyranny or chaos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Settle the seat of power and teach obedience
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a government requires... settle the seat of power, teach obedience, and the work is done.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establishing clear, respected institutions and inculcating obedience to magistrates and laws are prerequisites for effective government and for enabling acquisition and prosperity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders must not auction themselves for popularity
rubrics_metrics.description: When leaders choose to make themselves bidders at an auction of popularity, their talents, in the construction of the state, will be of no service; they become flatterers instead of legislators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid populist competition that rewards spectacle over prudence; leaders who pander will abandon moderation and compromise, undermining sound governance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moderation and compromise are essential virtues
rubrics_metrics.description: Moderation will be stigmatized as the virtue of cowards, and compromise as the prudence of traitors, until leaders are forced to propagate doctrines that later defeat sober purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practicing moderation and compromise is politically costly in the short term but necessary to temper extremes and secure long-term stable government; do not mistake popularity for good policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve useful tradition; alter only to preserve
rubrics_metrics.description: Let us preserve what our ancestors have left standing in our several reviews and reformations, and when we change, let it be to preserve — make the reparation as nearly as possible in the style of the building.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cautious, conservative reform that respects the established constitution (here, the British Constitution) is preferable to wholesale destruction and radical experimentation; follow the example of forefathers' prudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish real relief from destructive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: To tell the people that they are relieved by the dilapidation of their public estate is a cruel and insolent imposition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether measures that abolish institutions or public property actually benefit the people; do not conflate destruction of public assets with genuine relief — consider trade-offs between paying and gaining versus being disburdened.

rubrics_metrics.name: Superficial improvements do not justify fundamental errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of the regulations made by the Assembly were either conceded by the king or contained in prior instructions; some usages have been abolished on just grounds, but the improvements are superficial and the errors fundamental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beware reforms that change appearance but leave essential structures broken; radical action needs to be justified by necessity, not by opportunistic pretence of improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caution against the daring spirit of innovators
rubrics_metrics.description: A salutary lesson of caution against the daring spirit of innovators is furnished by the havoc caused in France by presumptuous good intentions of ignorance and incapacity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Innovation divorced from prudence and understanding can devastate public estate and societal stability; exercise conservative caution when altering foundational institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorities and laws must command reverence
rubrics_metrics.description: The magistrate must have his reverence, the laws their authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintaining respect for magistrates and legal authority is necessary for social order and for enabling productive industry; undermining authority destabilizes society.
